fields.title: GDP and GNP
fields.content: GNP: approximately $1.59 billion (2018). GDP heavily dependent on tourism. COVID-19 caused significant GDP collapse when tourism stopped. Upper-middle income country classification.

fields.title: Human Development Index
fields.content: HDI score: 0.796 (67th of 189 countries). The HDI is preferable to GNP as a measure of development because it includes health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling), and income — not just economic output.

fields.title: Currency and Exchange
fields.content: Seychelles Rupee (SCR). GNP is given in US dollars to allow international comparison between countries.

fields.title: Trade Memberships
fields.content: Seychelles belongs to: IOTC (Indian Ocean Tuna Commission), AU (African Union), SADC (Southern African Development Community), COMESA (Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa), WTO (World Trade Organization).

fields.title: Exports and Imports
fields.content: Exports: canned tuna, raw fish. Imports: fuel, electronics, clothing, motor vehicles, food products. EEZ (Exclusive Economic Zone): 1.37 million km2 — one of the largest in the world relative to land area.

fields.title: North-South Divide and Brandt Line
fields.content: The Brandt Line divides the world into the richer 'North' and poorer 'South'. Seychelles is in the Southern hemisphere but is classified as upper-middle income, showing the limitation of this simplistic division.

fields.title: Indian Ocean Tuna (IOT)
fields.content: IOT (Indian Ocean Tuna) is one of the world's largest tuna canneries and a major employer in Seychelles. Located on Mahe. Processes skipjack and yellowfin tuna for export, primarily to the European Union.

fields.title: Tourism Industry
fields.content: Tourism is the backbone of the Seychelles economy, contributing a large share of GDP. Seychelles positions itself as a premium, low-volume, high-value destination. The sector was severely impacted by COVID-19.

fields.title: Foodpro and Fishing
fields.content: Foodpro is the main food processing company in Seychelles. Fishing is divided into artisanal (small-scale, local consumption) and industrial (large-scale, export-oriented). Both are significant economic activities.

fields.title: Island Types
fields.content: Granitic Inner Islands (Mahe, Praslin, La Digue) — continental granite origin, mountainous and hilly. Coralline Outer Islands (Aldabra, Farquhar, Cosmoledo) — low-lying coral atolls formed on ancient coral reefs.

fields.title: Key Geographic Features
fields.content: Morne Seychellois: 905m, highest peak on Mahe and in Seychelles. Capital: Victoria, on the northeast coast of Mahe. Victoria is one of the smallest capital cities in the world.

fields.title: Land and Sea Area
fields.content: Total land area: approximately 459 km2 spread across 115 islands. EEZ: 1.37 million km2. The ocean territory is nearly 3,000 times larger than the land area.

fields.title: Tropical Maritime Climate
fields.content: Tropical maritime climate with two distinct seasons. North-west monsoon (October-April): hot, wet, calmer seas. South-east trade winds (May-September): cooler, drier, windier. No true dry season — rain falls year-round.

fields.title: Temperature and Rainfall
fields.content: Annual rainfall in Victoria: approximately 2,300mm. Temperature range: 24-30 degrees Celsius year-round. Higher elevations on Mahe receive significantly more rainfall than coastal areas.

fields.title: Population Demographics
fields.content: Population: approximately 98,000 people. About 90% live on Mahe. Significant immigrant workforce in construction and tourism sectors. Ethnically diverse population of Creole, European, Asian, and African descent.

fields.title: Languages
fields.content: Three official languages: Seychellois Creole (Kreol), English, and French. Creole is the most widely spoken language in daily life. English is the medium of instruction in schools.

fields.title: Marine Conservation
fields.content: Seychelles has established extensive marine protected areas covering approximately 30% of its ocean territory. The country conducted a debt-for-nature swap with Paris Club creditors, converting national debt into conservation funding.

fields.title: UNESCO World Heritage Sites
fields.content: Vallee de Mai on Praslin: home to the endemic coco de mer palm. Aldabra Atoll: the world's largest raised coral atoll, home to giant Aldabra tortoises. Both are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

fields.title: Renewable Energy and Blue Economy
fields.content: Seychelles has committed to generating 15% of energy from renewable sources. The 'Blue Economy' strategy focuses on sustainable use of ocean resources for economic growth while preserving marine ecosystems.

fields.title: OS Map Specifications
fields.content: Seychelles national exams use 1:10,000 scale topographic maps. Students must read grid references (4-figure and 6-figure), measure distances, identify contour patterns, and describe relief features from these maps.

fields.title: Map Areas Used in Exams
fields.content: Documented exam map areas: Cascade/Pointe Larue area (2023 exam), Beau Vallon area (2021 exam). Features include: Mahe coastal settlements, water treatment works, police stations, schools, jetties, steep granite terrain contours.

fields.title: Major Settlements
fields.content: Victoria (capital, NE Mahe), Anse Royale (SE Mahe), Beau Vallon (NW Mahe — major tourist beach), Baie Lazare (SW Mahe), Grand Anse (Praslin). Most settlements are coastal due to the mountainous interior.

fields.title: Employment Sectors
fields.content: Service sector (tourism, government) employs the majority. Industrial sector centres on tuna processing (IOT) and beverage manufacturing (SeyBrew). Agriculture is minimal — Seychelles imports most food.

fields.title: Environmental Challenges
fields.content: Key challenges: coral bleaching from rising sea temperatures, coastal erosion, limited freshwater resources, waste management on small islands, invasive species threatening endemic biodiversity.

fields.title: Trade Deficit
fields.content: Seychelles has a significant trade deficit — it imports far more than it exports. Main reason: small island economy with limited natural resources and manufacturing capacity. Tourism revenue helps offset the trade gap.
